facts.value: Monetarism emerged in the 1950s and 1960s, with Milton Friedman as its intellectual leader.
Monetarists contended that monetary policy and other monetary shocks, as represented by the growth in the money stock, were an important cause of economic fluctuations.
Monetary policy was considered more important than fiscal policy for purposes of stabilization.
Friedman was skeptical about the ability of central banks to conduct a sensible active monetary policy in practice, advocating instead using simple rules such as a steady rate of money growth.
Monetarism rose to prominence in the 1970s and 1980s, when several major central banks adopted monetarist-inspired policies.
Monetarism was later abandoned because the results were unsatisfactory.
